entries.summary: Commentary critiques Plato's proposals regarding communal property, state-controlled breeding, and the abolition of natural families, emphasizing human agency over rigid determinism. It further assesses the philosophical limitations and merits of equating political entities with individual moral agents.

entries.label: Glaucon on Contract and Gyges
entries.summary: Glaucon outlines the view of justice as an involuntary compromise designed to avoid suffering harm, using the myth of the Gyges ring to argue that unchecked power inevitably leads to injustice.

entries.label: Socratic City Construction
entries.summary: Socrates proposes studying justice on a larger scale within the state, constructing a society based on natural aptitude and the division of labor. He notes that expanding desires introduce war, requiring careful education and censorship of corrupting mythical tales for youthful guardians.

entries.label: Moral Ideals and Truth in Soul
entries.summary: Commentary on the early books examines the defense of justice as an ennobling ideal independent of external circumstances, alongside the distinction between medicinal fictions and the corrupting lie in the soul.

entries.label: Dialectic and the Cave Rulers
entries.summary: These passages address the philosophical education culminating in dialectic as the coping-stone of sciences, the nature of abstract thinking, and the dual disorders of eyesight faced when compelling enlightened philosophers to descend into the cave to govern.

entries.label: Constitutional and Moral Decay
entries.summary: Socrates and the commentator outline the four degenerate forms of government—timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny—and their corresponding human types, tracking an ethical gradation from reason down to a tyrannical monster passion.

entries.label: Pleasure, Soul, and City Pattern
entries.summary: Discussions analyze the tripartite soul using the image of the man, lion, and many-headed beast, establish the rational hierarchy of pleasures, and present the ideal city as an internal celestial pattern for individual self-governance.

entries.label: Ideals, Poetry, and Statesmanship
entries.summary: Commentary addresses Plato's rejection of imitative poetry in favor of universals, the nature of the ideal Republic as an unattainable vision rather than an earthly reality, the practical tensions of the philosopher-statesman, and modern dual ideals reconciled through faith.

entries.label: Virtue, Harm, and Happiness
entries.summary: In Book I dialogue, Socrates argues that justice can never involve harming others and demonstrates that because a just soul lives well, the just person is inherently happy and profitable while the unjust person is miserable.

entries.label: Body, Soul, and Medical Care
entries.summary: These commentaries examine the relationship between physical and mental well-being, exploring the harmonization of spirited and rational faculties through music and gymnastics while critiquing Plato's views on bodily medicine and gradual healing.

entries.label: Civic Good and Priority of Duty
entries.summary: This selection discusses state governance, arguing that political order aims at the happiness and excellence of the whole commonwealth rather than any single faction, with moral duty and fundamental education taking precedence over piecemeal statutes.

entries.label: Harmonic Order in Soul and State
entries.summary: These passages define justice and civic unity across the tripartite soul and the state, describing how functional division of labor and mutual harmony enable both the individual psyche and the polis to operate as integrated organisms.

entries.label: Philosopher-Rulers and Society
entries.summary: Socrates proposes that just governance requires uniting political rule with philosophy, while also warning of the acute vulnerability of noble philosophic characters to corruption by public pressure and popular opinion.

entries.label: Epistemology and the Good
entries.summary: This sequence articulates Plato's central metaphysical and epistemological doctrines, distinguishing knowledge from opinion and employing the analogies of the Sun, the Divided Line, and the Cave to chart the soul's ascent toward the supreme Idea of the Good.

entries.label: Lifelong Education and Ideals
entries.summary: These later overview sections examine the broader significance of Platonic philosophy, highlighting education as a lifelong redirection of the soul toward the light and considering how transcendent ideals—including the Idea of the Good and the concept of the Divine Man—elevate human conduct.

entries.label: Education and Poetic Forms
entries.summary: Discussions center on foundational civic training, addressing theological principles of divine goodness, poetic modes of imitation and narration, and the essential role of musical simplicity and harmony in shaping virtuous character.

entries.label: State Structure and the Soul
entries.summary: This grouping links psychological principles—such as non-contradiction—with the composition and governance of the state, including civic unity, the parable of the ship of state, and the direct correspondence between regime types and individual characters.

entries.label: Epistemology and Forms
entries.summary: These passages define cognitive faculties, contrast the unified nature of ideal Forms with the fluctuating ambiguities of sensory particulars, and evaluate ideals as enduring standards beyond imperfect earthly realizations.

entries.label: The Good and the Cave Allegory
entries.summary: Socrates establishes the supreme knowledge of the Good through the analogy of the sun, presenting the allegory of prisoners in the cave and detailing their arduous perceptual ascent to the illuminating source of reality.

entries.label: Virtue and the Soul in State
entries.summary: Socrates establishes divine immutability and truthfulness as ethical standards while defining civic temperance, justice, and the tripartite division of the soul in terms of harmonious order and proper function.

entries.label: Philosopher-Kings and Epistemology
entries.summary: Socrates introduces the rule of philosophers and rigorously distinguishes true knowledge of eternal forms from the fallible opinions of dreamers who focus on sensory particulars.

entries.label: Reality, Pleasure, and Destiny
entries.summary: Across later books, Socrates divides intelligible and visible reality, exposes intermediate rest as an illusion of pleasure, and illustrates the soul's fateful choices and rebirth in the myth of Er.

entries.label: Editorial Syntheses of Themes
entries.summary: Editorial notes synthesize Plato's central metaphysical and ethical doctrines, covering dialectical method, divine nature, the Idea of the Good, civic and psychic justice, and Platonic psychology.

entries.label: Civic Order and Soul Harmony
entries.summary: Socrates describes justice and virtue as internal systemic harmonies balancing bodily and spirited elements within both individuals and the state. Proper civic arrangement directs diverse natures toward collective well-being rather than segmented benefit.

entries.label: Nature and Education of Rulers
entries.summary: Discussions center on the innate disposition of true philosophers and the societal corruptions that deform their development under ordinary regimes. Socrates prescribes a rigorous, lifelong educational scheme to protect potential rulers and reconcile public suspicion with genuine wisdom.

entries.label: Dialectical Ascent and Rule
entries.summary: Dialectic is distinguished from hypothetical sciences as the supreme study ascending directly to the first principle and the Good. Once philosophers attain this vision, they must return to civic governance to order the commonwealth justly.

entries.label: Critique of Mimetic Poetry
entries.summary: Socrates rejects imitative arts, arguing they produce illusions twice removed from truth and foster irrational passions within the human soul. This longstanding conflict between philosophy and poetry permits the latter's return only if its moral utility can be demonstrated.

entries.label: Epistemology and Soul Ascent
entries.summary: Reason moves through dialectical inquiry and cognitive faculties to comprehend the highest realities. Education operates by redirecting the soul's intrinsic vision away from the sensible domain toward the realm of true being and the good.

entries.label: Desires, Pleasures, and Regimes
entries.summary: Desires and pleasures are distinguished between necessary benefits and corrupting excesses, reflecting political shifts from uncontrolled liberty to tyranny. The tripartite structure of the soul demonstrates that the virtuous life produces genuine satisfaction over illusory physical appetites.

entries.label: Internal Rule and Justice
entries.summary: The human soul is characterized as a composite of beast, lion, and rational mind, showing that justice demands subjection of appetite to divine reason. Living by an internal pattern of order aligns personal conduct with ideal law regardless of outer circumstance.

entries.label: Imitation and Reality
entries.summary: Reality is analyzed across levels of divine form, physical craft, and artistic imitation. Knowledge belongs to the user and correct belief to the maker, leaving the imitator detached from genuine understanding.

entries.label: Soul's Immortality and Rewards
entries.summary: Because moral vice fails to dissolve the soul, it is proven to be immortal and inherently akin to the divine when stripped of bodily encrustations. With its intrinsic goodness established, justice is also acknowledged to receive supreme external honors and divine favor.

entries.label: Republic Commentary & Dialectic
entries.summary: These commentaries survey the macro-structure and philosophical evolution of the Republic, charting the trajectory of moral definitions, the demands placed upon justice, and Plato's deductive dialectic in relation to ancient and modern methods of thought and artistic critique.

entries.label: Ideal City and Guardianship
entries.summary: These accounts outline the construction of the ideal polity through the state-individual analogy, detailing guardian selection, early educational censorship, communal institutions, and the advanced curriculum designed to elevate dialectical philosopher-rulers.

entries.label: Degeneration and Mysticism
entries.summary: These passages examine the political and psychological decline of states and individuals from timocracy to tyranny, the extreme misery of the tyrannical man, and the symbolic cosmological and mathematical formulas embedded in Plato's mythological visions.

entries.label: Comparative Political Polities
entries.summary: These analyses review the foundational models, radical institutional paradoxes, and Spartan influences in Plato's Republic, tracing how its vision of governance compares with other Platonic texts and subsequent historical political traditions.

entries.label: Dialectical Search for Justice
entries.summary: Following opening discussions on wealth and moral duty, Socrates encounters aporia when assessing the profits of justice before defining its essence, prompting Adeimantus to demand an evaluation of how justice and injustice intrinsically shape the soul.

entries.label: Guardian Curricular Governance
entries.summary: In structuring civic guardian education, Socrates prescribes strict limits on narrative representations of death and statecraft deceit, while eliminating mournful and complex musical modes in favour of sober, temperate harmonies and simple instruments.

entries.label: Civic Class Roles & Guardian Life
entries.summary: Socrates establishes civic virtues through functional specialization, judicial observation, and class division reinforced by the Myth of the Metals. Stringent curbs on dramatic imitation and private property are placed upon the guardians, prompting Adeimantus to question whether defenders denied personal wealth can be happy.

entries.label: Gender, Community & Warfare
entries.summary: In response to Adeimantus's interruptions regarding the sharing of women and children, Socrates proposes equal education and administrative roles for women and establishes communal family structures to maximize civic cohesion. He further prescribes regulations governing inter-Hellenic conflict, distinguishing internal discord from foreign war.

entries.label: Philosopher-Kings & Curriculum
entries.summary: Socrates defines true philosophers by their devotion to eternal truth rather than sensory imitations, defending the feasibility of philosopher-rulers over corrupt alternatives. To educate them, he lays out a rigorous higher curriculum progressing through mathematical sciences to dialectic, guarded by strict age requirements.

entries.label: Regime Decline & True Pleasure
entries.summary: Socrates charts the generational degeneration of regimes and corresponding psychological types through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny. He contrasts the enslaved, miserable existence of the tyrant with the superior, unmixed pleasures experienced by the philosopher, concluding with mathematical comparisons of their respective happiness.

entries.label: Editorial Apparatus & Notes
entries.summary: Modern editorial commentary and index entries synthesize Plato's views on poetry, art censorship, guardian requirements, and the composite historical elements of the ideal state. In addition, transcriber editorial notes explain typographic adjustments, collation practices, and Greek transliteration systems.

entries.label: Early Foundations and Soul Care
entries.summary: These commentaries examine the introductory definitions of justice, social contract theory, and political origins, balancing external rules with the moral purity of the soul. They address the lie in the soul and explore the harmonization of reason and physical nature through gymnastics, music, and medical restraint.

entries.label: Civic Order and Soul Harmony
entries.summary: These passages define justice and civic unity across both the individual soul and the commonwealth, establishing that political order aims at the good of the whole rather than sectional interest. Functional division of labor and the harmony of the tripartite soul enable both psyche and state to operate as integrated organisms.

entries.label: Philosopher-Kings and the Good
entries.summary: This sequence addresses the core paradox of philosopher-rulers and their vulnerability to social corruption, alongside the metaphysical distinction between knowledge and opinion. It details the ascent to the supreme Idea of the Good via the Sun, Line, and Cave analogies, culminating in dialectical education and the compelled return to govern.

entries.label: Political Decay and Pleasures
entries.summary: These discussions trace the progressive decline of constitutions and character from timocracy to tyranny, tracking the moral deterioration driven by master passions. They contrast this disorder with the rational hierarchy of pleasures, the composite image of the soul, and the celestial pattern of the ideal city.

entries.label: Critiques and Broader Ideals
entries.summary: These commentaries critique Plato's radical social proposals—such as the abolition of families and state breeding—while analyzing his banishment of imitative poetry and the state-individual analogy. They explore Platonic thought as a visionary framework for lifelong self-education, abstract universals, and transcendent ideals.

entries.label: Book I Dialogues on Justice
entries.summary: Socrates engages with Polemarchus and Thrasymachus regarding whether justice serves the stronger ruler, harms enemies, or produces advantage. Through the craft analogy and arguments on civic discord, Socrates establishes that arts serve their subjects and that justice is the vital excellence and happiness of the soul.

entries.label: Book II Contract and City Genesis
entries.summary: Glaucon restates the case for injustice using the classification of goods, social contract theory, and the Gyges ring thought experiment. In response, Socrates initiates the large-letter analogy of the state, tracing the genesis of society from human interdependence to the luxurious city requiring guardian censorship.

entries.label: Virtue, Soul, and Civic Order
entries.summary: Socrates establishes ethical, theological, and aesthetic standards through early education, music, and divine principles. These disciplines form the foundation for civic temperance and justice, establishing harmonious proportion across the tripartite soul and classes of the state.

entries.label: Philosopher-Kings and the Forms
entries.summary: Socrates links state governance with psychological rigor, justifying the controversial paradox of philosopher-kings. True philosophers are distinguished from lovers of opinion by their cognitive grasp of eternal Forms, requiring protective education against social corruption.

entries.label: The Good, Cave, and Dialectic
entries.summary: Knowledge of the ultimate Good is framed through the Sun analogy and the Cave allegory, describing the soul's ascent from shadows to intellectual truth. Dialectic is exalted as the unhypothetical coping-stone that equips enlightened philosophers to descend and justly govern.

entries.label: Regimes, Pleasures, and Reason
entries.summary: Socrates analyzes the four degraded constitutions alongside their corresponding character types, showing how unchecked appetite precipitates tyranny. Psychological proofs demonstrate that true satisfaction and justice depend on subjecting appetitive elements to the inner divine rule of reason.

entries.label: Poetry and Mimetic Illusion
entries.summary: Imitative art is critically dissected as a thrice-removed copy lacking genuine knowledge of reality. Socrates banishes mimetic poetry for catering to the irrational, grieving aspects of the soul, welcoming it back only if its moral benefit can be defended in prose.

entries.label: Immortality and Eschatology
entries.summary: Socrates argues for the indestructible immortality of the soul, revealing its pure nature apart from bodily afflictions. External rewards and cosmic justice are affirmed through the myth of Er, which depicts post-mortem judgment, tenfold retribution, and the fateful choice of future lives.

entries.label: Editorial Apparatus & Notes
entries.summary: Covers publication prefaces, dedications, acknowledgments, transcriber conventions, and synthesized modern editorial index notes on Plato's political and artistic theories.

entries.label: Macro-Analyses and Influences
entries.summary: Broad essays examine the architecture and dialectic of the Republic, compare Plato's ideal polity with Spartan and subsequent historical utopias, and trace the psychological and cosmological dimensions of regime degeneration.

entries.label: Foundations of Justice & City
entries.summary: Beginning with the aporia over justice and the demand to examine its inherent nature in the soul, these sections trace the construction of the ideal city and the early curricular censorship required to train guardian protectors.

entries.label: Guardian Society & Leadership
entries.summary: Details the division of classes through the Myth of the Metals, communal institutions including the equality of women and shared families, and the advanced dialectical and mathematical curriculum designed to produce philosopher-kings.

entries.label: Regime Decline & Afterlife
entries.summary: Socrates traces the decay of states into tyranny alongside the misery of the tyrannical man, culminating in the cosmological vision of the Spindle of Necessity and the afterlife rewards of justice.

entries.label: Commentaries on Platonic Thought
entries.summary: This sequence gathers extensive philosophical commentaries analyzing the core themes of the Republic, spanning early ethical foundations and the care of the soul, civic harmony and functional order, and the metaphysics of philosopher-kings and the Idea of the Good. They evaluate the progressive decline of political regimes and soul types alongside critical appraisals of Plato's radical social institutions, educational models, and transcendent ideals.

entries.label: Origins of Justice and the State
entries.summary: These dialogues cover Books I through IV, examining initial debates on whether justice serves the stronger and exploring the genesis of the state from basic needs to a luxurious commonwealth. They chart the formation of civic harmony, censorship of narratives, and musical and gymnastic education that align the tripartite soul with civic classes.

entries.label: Philosopher-Kings and Metaphysics
entries.summary: Focusing on Books V through VII, these passages examine the paradox of the philosopher-king, the distinction between true knowledge of eternal Forms and mere opinion, and the corruption of gifted natures. They elaborate the ascent to the Idea of the Good through the Sun, Divided Line, and Cave allegories, culminating in dialectic as the highest science.

entries.label: Regimes, Poetry, and Immortality
entries.summary: Covering the later books and editorial summaries, these sections investigate constitutional degeneration into tyranny, the psychological proofs of rational pleasure, and the banishment of mimetic poetry as an appeal to the inferior soul. They conclude with arguments for the immortality of the soul, cosmic retribution in the myth of Er, and overarching editorial syntheses of Platonic doctrines.

entries.label: Commentary on Dialectic & State
entries.summary: These analytical essays and critical commentaries examine the structural architecture and core philosophical doctrines of the Republic. They trace the evolution of Platonic ethics, the metaphysics of the philosopher-king and the Good, comparative utopian traditions, and regime decay.

entries.label: Genesis of Justice and State
entries.summary: Focusing on Books I through IV, these dialogues and commentaries explore initial disputes regarding justice, its definition in the soul, and the construction of the primitive through luxurious commonwealth. They chart early civic education, theological and poetic censorship, and the alignment of the tripartite soul with civic virtues.

entries.label: Philosopher-Kings & Metaphysics
entries.summary: Focusing on Books V through VII, these sections detail the communal institutions of the guardian class, the equality of women, and the central paradox of the philosopher-king. They articulate the metaphysical ascent from opinion to knowledge of the Forms and the Idea of the Good via mathematics and dialectic.

entries.label: Constitutional Decay & Immortality
entries.summary: These texts cover Books VIII through X, examining the psychological and political degeneration of regimes from timocracy to tyranny, the nature of true pleasure, and the banishment of mimetic poetry. They conclude with demonstrations of the soul's immortality and the cosmic vision of retribution in the Myth of Er.
